scope: Evidence lines for self-designed Movefield workouts: hypertrophy and volume, rest, strength and powerlifting, powerbuilding, jump and power, running and concurrent training, sport strength, beginner adult guidance, and youth gaps.
registry: app/page.tsx SOURCE_LINKS. Existing keys were checked for duplicates before any new key was proposed.
method: Each record was checked against a primary page where the page was readable. PubMed web pages returned a bot-check page and the NCBI E-utilities host was refused by the egress proxy, so PubMed-derived records were read from the Europe PMC REST API. Publisher, PMC, journal and organisation pages were read where they loaded. Pages refused by rate limits or access controls are listed under notConfirmed. Summaries use abstract-level wording only and avoid effect sizes that were not in the abstract text read.

sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) with title, authors, journal, year, DOI and abstract wording. The DOI page returned 403 and the PubMed page returned a bot check.
sources.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis reporting a graded dose-response relationship between weekly resistance-training volume and muscle hypertrophy.
notVerified: Full text and study counts not read; the summary uses the abstract's wording only.

sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
sources.verifiedVia: Springer article page (title, authors, journal, year, volume, pages, DOI, abstract conclusions). PMID taken from a PubMed link in search results, not read on PubMed.
sources.summary: Across volume-matched comparisons, training each muscle group twice a week was associated with greater hypertrophy than once a week; the authors state that whether three times a week is superior remains to be determined.
notVerified: Effect sizes in the abstract were not transcribed; the summary avoids them.

sources.authors: Grgic J, Schoenfeld BJ, Davies TB, Lazinica B, Krieger JW, Pedisic Z
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) with authors, journal, year, DOI, PMID and abstract conclusions.
sources.summary: Higher weekly frequency was associated with larger strength gains, but the authors report that this appears driven mainly by training volume, and the frequency effect was not significant in the volume-equated subgroup.
notVerified: Specific effect-size values and per-frequency estimates not used.

sources.authors: Refalo MC, Helms ER, Trexler ET, Hamilton DL, Fyfe JJ
sources.verifiedVia: PubMed Central article page PMC9935748 (title, authors, journal, volume, pages, DOI, abstract conclusions and numbers).
sources.summary: A systematic review with meta-analysis found no evidence that training to momentary muscular failure is superior to non-failure training for hypertrophy; set-to-failure showed a trivial advantage (effect size 0.19), and the relation between proximity to failure and hypertrophy appears non-linear.
notVerified: Velocity-loss subgroup values not used.

sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) with authors, journal, year, DOI, PMID and abstract conclusions.
sources.summary: In a systematic review of studies in which all sets were taken to momentary failure, high-load training (above 60% 1RM) produced greater 1RM gains than low-load training, while hypertrophy changes were similar across loading ranges.
notVerified: Issue number not read; limited to studies with sets to failure, as the summary states.

sources.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Pope ZK, Benik FM, Hester GM, Sellers J, Nooner JL, Schnaiter JA, Bond-Williams KE, Carter AS, Ross CL, Just BL, Henselmans M, Krieger JW
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) and a journal-linked record with authors, journal, volume, pages, DOI and abstract findings.
sources.summary: In an 8-week randomized study of 21 resistance-trained men, 3-minute rests between sets produced greater 1RM squat and bench press gains and greater anterior-thigh muscle thickness than 1-minute rests.
notVerified: Single study with a small sample; the triceps result was a trend only, and the summary omits it.

sources.authors: Grgic J, Lazinica B, Mikulic P, Krieger JW, Schoenfeld BJ
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) with authors, journal, year, DOI, PMID and abstract conclusions.
sources.summary: A systematic review of six studies concluded that both short and long rest intervals may be useful for hypertrophy, with a possible advantage for long rests in trained participants, and that clearer differentiation needs further research.
notVerified: Individual study data not read.

sources.authors: Williams TD, Tolusso DV, Fedewa MV, Esco MR
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) with authors, journal, year, DOI, PMID and conclusion and results wording.
sources.summary: A meta-analysis reported that periodized resistance-training plans had a moderate effect on 1RM compared with non-periodized plans (effect size 0.43, 95% CI 0.27-0.58).
notVerified: A 2018 critical comment (PMID 29178086) and author reply (PMID 29178085) exist; neither was read, so their objections are not assessed.

sources.authors: Peterson MD, Rhea MR, Alvar BA
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) with title, authors, journal, year, DOI, PMID and the abstract's conclusion.
sources.summary: A meta-analysis of athletes reported that maximal strength gains were elicited among athletes training at a mean intensity of 85% of 1RM.
notVerified: Frequency and volume findings in the abstract were not read and are not cited here. The result applies to athletes, not to all trainees.

sources.authors: Suchomel TJ, Nimphius S, Bellon CR, Stone MH
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) with title, authors, journal, year, DOI, PMID and abstract conclusions.
sources.summary: A review of muscular strength for athletic performance that suggests training to failure is not likely required for maximal strength gains, multiple sets appear to outperform single sets, and weaker athletes should build strength before emphasizing power.
notVerified: Full text not read; the statements are abstract-level.

sources.authors: Wisloff U, Castagna C, Helgerud J, Jones R, Hoff J
sources.verifiedVia: PubMed Central article page PMC1724821 (title, authors, journal, volume, pages, DOI, PMID and abstract conclusion).
sources.summary: In 17 elite male soccer players, half-squat strength showed a strong correlation with sprint and jump performance; the authors write that squat strength 'determines' these outcomes, but the study is correlational and does not show that raising squat strength would improve them.
notVerified: Correlation coefficients were not in the abstract text read; none are quoted.

sources.authors: Markovic G
sources.pmid: 17347316 (seen in search results; not read on PubMed)
sources.verifiedVia: BJSM journal abstract page: single author, abstract conclusion and effect sizes read. Journal, volume and issue taken from the page URL. DOI not read.
sources.summary: A meta-analysis reporting that plyometric training gives a statistically significant improvement in vertical jump height, with abstract effect sizes of 0.44 (95% CI 0.15-0.72) for squat jump and 0.88 (95% CI 0.64-1.11) for countermovement jump.
notVerified: DOI and PMID not read on the journal page. Effect sizes come from a summarized fetch of the abstract and should be re-read against the page before they are quoted in the app.

sources.authors: Stojanovic E, Ristic V, McMaster DT, Milanovic Z
sources.verifiedVia: Springer article page (title, authors, journal, year, volume, pages, DOI and abstract results).
sources.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 studies in female athletes reports a moderate effect of plyometric training on countermovement-jump height (effect size 1.09, 95% CI 0.57-1.61, I2 75.6%), with larger effects in programs longer than 10 weeks.
notVerified: Participant totals not read. Heterogeneity is high and the squat-jump and drop-jump estimates have very wide intervals, so they are not quoted.

sources.authors: Schumann M, Feuerbacher JF, Sunkeler M, Freitag N, Ronnestad BR, Doma K, Lundberg TR
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) with title, authors, journal, year, DOI, PMID and the abstract's conclusion. The registry URL matches this DOI.
sources.summary: Across 43 studies, concurrent aerobic and strength training did not compromise muscle hypertrophy or maximal strength development, but explosive strength was attenuated, and more so when both modes were done in the same session.
notVerified: Individual study data and effect-size values not quoted.

sources.authors: Plotkin D, Coleman M, Van Every D, Maldonado J, Oberlin D, Israetel M, Feather J, Alto A, Vigotsky AD, Schoenfeld BJ
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) with title, authors, journal, year, DOI, PMID and the abstract's conclusion.
sources.summary: An 8-week comparison concluded that both repetition progression and load progression appear to be viable strategies for muscular adaptation.
notVerified: Registry summary emphasizes repetitions; the abstract treats both routes as viable. Consider aligning the registry wording.

sources.authors: Iversen VM, Norum M, Schoenfeld BJ, Fimland MS
sources.verifiedVia: Europe PMC REST record (PubMed-derived) with title, authors, journal, year, DOI, PMID and abstract conclusions.
sources.summary: A narrative review, not an experiment, concluding that weekly training volume is more important than training frequency, and suggesting a minimum of four weekly sets per muscle group using a 6-15 RM range for time-efficient programs.
notVerified: The registry summary's claim that short focused sessions can distribute training across the week was not seen in the abstract text read.

sources.authors: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, Borodulin K, Buman MP, Cardon G, Carty C, Chaput JP, Chastin S, Chou R, Dempsey PC, DiPietro L, Ekelund U, Firth J, Friedenreich CM, Garcia L, Gichu M, Jago R, Katzmarzyk PT, Lambert E, Leitzmann M, Milton K, Ortega FB, Ranasinghe C, Stamatakis E, Tiedemann A, Troiano RP, van der Ploeg HP, Wari V, Willumsen JF
sources.verifiedVia: PubMed Central article page PMC7719906 (title, all 31 authors, journal, volume, pages, DOI and the recommendation text). The WHO publication page confirmed title and year only.
sources.summary: Adults aged 18-64 should do at least 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (or 75-150 minutes vigorous) per week, plus muscle-strengthening activity at moderate or greater intensity on at least 2 days a week; children and adolescents aged 5-17 should average at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity, with muscle- and bone-strengthening at least 3 days a week.
notVerified: The youth 3-days-per-week figure was read from the Table 4 summary; the narrative text does not give the same number.

sources.authors: NHS (organisation page, no individual authors)
sources.verifiedVia: NHS page read directly: 3 runs a week, a rest day between runs, the week 1-3 run/walk structure, 9-week duration, and permission to repeat a week.
sources.summary: A public-health 9-week run/walk plan with three runs a week, a rest day between runs, and permission to repeat a week or run when needed.
notVerified: No peer-reviewed trial of this plan was found or checked; this is a public-health program page, not outcome evidence.

sources.authors: American College of Sports Medicine (public summary page; author not named on the page; Stuart M. Phillips is quoted as an author of the underlying position stand)
sources.journal: ACSM public webpage (position stand summary, dated 2026-03-17)
sources.verifiedVia: ACSM public summary page read. The full position stand was not read.
sources.summary: ACSM's March 2026 public summary states that training to fatigue or momentary muscle failure did not consistently affect outcomes for average healthy adults, and that training all major muscle groups at least twice a week matters more than pursuing a complex plan.
notVerified: 'Consistent progressive training matters' was not found on the public page; the page gives no progression guidance. The 80% 1RM for 2-3 sets, about 10 weekly sets per muscle group and 30-70% 1RM power loads were read from the summary and not confirmed in the full stand.

sources.authors: Lloyd RS, Cronin JB, Faigenbaum AD, Haff GG, Howard R, Kraemer WJ, Micheli LJ, Myer GD, Oliver JL
sources.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
sources.verifiedVia: NSCA organisation page read: authors, journal, volume, issue and month. The full statement and DOI were not read.
sources.summary: An NSCA position statement that youth should be physically active and treated as athletes, with individualized, holistic and child-centred development that reduces injury risk and builds lifelong habits.
notVerified: Full statement, DOI and page numbers not read; summary is from the NSCA page.

sources.authors: Bergeron MF et al. (18 authors; first author confirmed on page)
sources.verifiedVia: BJSM page read: title ('International Olympic Committee consensus statement on youth athletic development'), first author, and conclusions confirmed. Journal and year taken from the URL volume (49); not stated in the fetched text. DOI not read.
sources.summary: A consensus statement that youth athletic development should be assessed individually, early specialization should be avoided in favour of varied sport, and training load should be balanced with rest and recovery.
notVerified: Full author list, DOI and year not read on the page.

sources.authors: Barbell Medicine (site and publisher; no individual author named on page)
sources.verifiedVia: Barbell Medicine powerlifting programs page read: maximal-strength focus on squat, bench and deadlift; site named as publisher; research cited in a numbered reference list (about 44 sources).
sources.summary: Expert program page focused on maximal strength in the squat, bench press and deadlift. It cites research in a reference list, but the page is expert opinion, not a trial.
notVerified: The cited references were not checked individually.

sources.authors: Barbell Medicine (site and publisher; no individual author named on page)
sources.verifiedVia: Barbell Medicine powerbuilding programs page read: described as a hybrid of powerlifting and bodybuilding; 31 numbered references cited.
sources.summary: Expert powerbuilding page describing programs for combined muscle size and strength in the squat, bench press and deadlift. It states that a hybrid approach may help trainees progress toward both goals faster; this claim is expert opinion and was not confirmed by a trial in this check.
notVerified: The 'progress faster' claim has no verified trial behind it; the 31 references were not checked.

sources.authors: Jeff Nippard (Jeff Nippard Fitness)
sources.verifiedVia: Product page read: creator named, program for beginner to intermediate lifters, paid ($39.99 USD), described as a simple linear progression.
sources.summary: A paid commercial hypertrophy program by its creator, described as a simple linear progression for beginner to intermediate lifters. It is expert product material, not research, and requires creator attribution.
notVerified: No routines or research claims from the product were checked; none are reproduced.

notConfirmed.candidate: Lesinski M, Prieske O, Granacher U. Effects and dose-response relationships of resistance training on physical performance in youth athletes. BJSM 2016;50:781-795 (youth dose-response meta-analysis)
notConfirmed.reason: The BJSM page at volume 50, issue 13, page 781 was read: the abstract conclusions were visible and the contributor initials (ML, OP, UG) matched. The fetched text did not show the title, year or DOI, and a second record check was refused by the proxy's rate limit. Excluded until the header and DOI are checked. It would fill the youth dose-response gap.

notConfirmed.candidate: Wilson JM et al. 2012. Concurrent training: a meta-analysis examining interference of aerobic and resistance exercises. JSCR 26(8):2293-2307
notConfirmed.reason: Not located in searches; the Europe PMC record was refused by the rate limit. CONCURRENT (Schumann 2022, verified) covers the interference question.

notConfirmed.candidate: Schoenfeld BJ et al. 2014. Effects of different volume-equated resistance training loading strategies on muscular adaptations in well-trained men. JSCR 28(10):2909-2918
notConfirmed.reason: Found only as a PDF and secondary pages. The primary record was refused by the rate limit. Would have supported the powerbuilding loading comparison.

notConfirmed.candidate: Behm DG, Faigenbaum AD, Falk B, Klentrou P. Canadian Society for Exercise Physiology position paper on resistance training for children and adolescents (Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism)
notConfirmed.reason: Only repository and secondary pages were found (Brock University record, SFU PDF). No journal page or DOI was retrieved, and the record fetch was refused.

notConfirmed.candidate: Grgic J et al. 2020. Effects of interset rest intervals on adaptations to resistance training: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Sports Medicine)
notConfirmed.reason: Searches did not return this record. The verified Grgic 2017 EJSS review (GRGIC-2017-REST) is cited instead.

Searches returned a UK observational paper on beginner runner programmes and non-completion (PMC10487403), which was not read. No randomized run/walk trial was verified. The NHS plan is the only verified run/walk progression source.

notConfirmed.candidate: Squat, bench and deadlift specificity or transfer between lifts
notConfirmed.reason: No primary study was verified. The NSCA Strength and Conditioning Journal transfer-between-lifts PDF (2022) was seen but not read, and it is a magazine-style article rather than a primary study. Specificity claims should rely on PL-EXPERT (expert opinion) until a source is verified.

notConfirmed.candidate: A trial of a combined strength and hypertrophy (powerbuilding-format) program
notConfirmed.reason: No direct trial was verified. Powerbuilding claims currently rest on indirect loading, frequency, failure and periodization evidence plus PB-EXPERT, which is expert opinion.

notConfirmed.candidate: Evidence for once-weekly bodyweight jump practice (the app's jumping focus)
notConfirmed.reason: None of the verified jump sources tests a once-weekly practice dose. The app's current once-a-week jump add-on is not supported by a verified source.
AAP-2020, NSCA-YOUTH, SEX-RESPONSE, OLDER-ADULT, ACSM-2009, EXERCISE-DATA. Not requested for these areas. Only AAP-2020 and NSCA-YOUTH are treated as existing youth coverage, as the brief specified.

gaps: No verified primary source for squat, bench or deadlift specificity.
No verified trial for the powerbuilding combined format.
No verified source for once-weekly jump practice.
No verified peer-reviewed run/walk trial beyond the NHS plan.
Youth dose-response (Lesinski 2016) is not confirmed; the youth gap is partly filled by WHO-2020 and LLOYD-2016-LTAD.
